chunks: And from him, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd, from al-Naḍr ibn Suwayd, from ʿĀṣim ibn Ḥumayd, from Abī Baṣīr, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
Whoever claims that Allah is from a thing, or in a thing, or upon a thing, has indeed committed kufr.
I said: Explain it to me.
He said: I mean by that a thing containing Him, or holding Him, or that He came from something that preceded Him.

And in another narration: Whoever claims that Allah is from a thing has made Him originated; whoever claims that He is in a thing has made Him confined; and whoever claims that He is upon a thing has made Him carried.
Concerning His, the Exalted, saying: “And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God in the earth.”

key_terms.إِلَهٌ: God, the one truly worthy of divinity
key_terms.الْحَوَايَةِ: containment or encompassment of something over Him
key_terms.بِإِمْسَاكٍ: being held or sustained by something else
key_terms.كَفَرَ: committed kufr by affirming a belief contrary to divine transcendence
key_terms.مَحْمُولًا: borne or carried by something else

ai.seo_question: What does this hadith teach about denying that Allah is in, from, or upon created things?
ai.summary: This hadith rejects any belief that Allah is derived from, contained within, or supported by created things. It affirms divine transcendence and explains that such descriptions would imply createdness, limitation, or dependence. The cited Qur'anic phrase is understood in a way consistent with tawhid and Allah’s absolute incomparability.
